subject: chemistry
title: Practical: investigating rates of reaction
key_idea: Rate can be followed by the volume of gas made, the mass lost, or the time for a mixture to go cloudy or change colour. Change one factor, keep every other variable the same, and record results at set times.

blocks.text: The method depends on what the reaction does. This section covers the three common methods and their apparatus.

rows: Volume of gas
A gas is made, such as hydrogen or carbon dioxide
Volume of gas at set times, or the time to collect a fixed volume
Gas syringe (or measuring cylinder and water trough), stopwatch
Mass lost
A gas escapes from the flask
Mass of the flask and contents at set times
Balance, stopwatch
Colour change or turbidity
A precipitate makes the mixture cloudy
Time for a cross to disappear, or light reaching a light sensor
Conical flask on a cross, stopwatch or light sensor

items: In the **mass lost** method, the gas escapes from the flask, so the mass goes down.
This method fails if the gas has a very small mass. 0.1 g of magnesium makes only 0.008 g of hydrogen, which is too small to measure accurately.
In the **turbidity** method, sodium thiosulfate reacts with hydrochloric acid to make a precipitate of sulfur. The mixture becomes cloudy.
A shorter time for the cross to disappear means a faster reaction.

blocks.label: Sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid
where: S(s) is the solid sulfur that makes the mixture cloudy

diagram.alt: Change the concentration of acid and the time to see the volume of gas collected in a gas syringe. A simple model: the rate is proportional to the concentration and stays constant until the syringe is full. A real rate falls as the reactants are used up.

items: Gas made: collect it in a gas syringe and time it. Gas lost: use a balance.
A precipitate makes a mixture cloudy: time how long until a cross cannot be seen.
The mass method needs a gas with enough mass to measure.

sections.heading: Investigating the effect of changing a condition

blocks.text: Change one variable at a time and keep everything else the same. This makes the investigation a fair test.

items.meaning: The one thing you change, such as concentration.
What you measure, such as time or volume of gas.
Something you keep the same so the test is fair.

items.text: Measure a volume of sodium thiosulfate solution and put it in a conical flask. Measure a volume of hydrochloric acid separately.
Place the flask on a cross drawn on paper, or use a light sensor.
Add the acid, swirl, and start the stopwatch.
Measure the time until the cross is no longer visible.
Repeat and find a mean. Then change the concentration by changing the ratio of thiosulfate volume to water volume.

items: Keep the concentration and the volume of hydrochloric acid the same.
Keep the total volume of sodium thiosulfate solution the same, adding water to dilute it.
**Temperature:** keep the flask in a water bath at the chosen temperature. Warm water alone is not enough, and a Bunsen burner is not used.
**Surface area:** use the same mass of marble chips in different sizes. Crush large chips in a pestle and mortar and sort them with sieves.
Keep the volume and concentration of acid and the mass of solid the same.
Change one independent variable. Keep the control variables the same.
For a dilution, change the volume of thiosulfate and water but keep the total volume constant.
Use a water bath to control temperature.

blocks.text: Careful measuring and repeats make results accurate and reliable.

items: Measure volumes with a measuring cylinder, pipette or burette.
A smaller measuring cylinder or a gas syringe has smaller gradations, so it gives a more precise volume than a large measuring cylinder.
Start the stopwatch as soon as the reactants are mixed. Swirl the flask.
Repeat each experiment and calculate a mean.
Say the reaction has finished when the solid has gone or there are no more bubbles.
Choose apparatus with small gradations for a precise measurement.
Repeat and find a mean.
Start timing as soon as the reactants mix.

checks.q: Name two pieces of apparatus used to find the rate of production of a gas.
checks.a: A gas syringe (or measuring cylinder and water trough) and a stopwatch.

checks.q: Explain why the mixture becomes cloudy when sodium thiosulfate reacts with hydrochloric acid.
checks.a: Sulfur is formed. It is a solid precipitate.

checks.q: A student investigates how temperature affects the reaction between magnesium and acid. State how to keep the acid at 40 °C.
checks.a: Place the conical flask in a water bath at 40 °C.

worked_example.question:
Sodium thiosulfate solution reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid, becoming cloudy as the reaction proceeds.

Plan an investigation to show how the concentration of the sodium thiosulfate solution affects the rate of the reaction with dilute hydrochloric acid.

Your plan should give valid results.
answer_points: Measure a volume of sodium thiosulfate and place it in a conical flask.
Measure a volume of hydrochloric acid.
Place the flask on a cross (or between a light source and a light sensor).
Add the hydrochloric acid, swirl, and start a stopwatch.
Measure the time for the cross to become no longer visible.
Repeat and find the mean.
Repeat for different concentrations of sodium thiosulfate, by changing the ratio of thiosulfate volume to water volume.
Control variables: concentration of the hydrochloric acid, volume of the hydrochloric acid, and total volume of sodium thiosulfate solution.
worked_example.tip: This is a levels question. Marks go for the key steps in a logical order and for naming the control variables.

worked_example.question:
Sodium thiosulfate solution, Na₂S₂O₃, reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid.

Na₂S₂O₃(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + SO₂(g) + S(s)

In an investigation, different concentrations of hydrochloric acid are reacted with sodium thiosulfate solution. The mixture goes cloudy at different rates.

Describe how the rate at which the mixture goes cloudy can be measured.
answer_points: Place the flask over (or in front of) a cross.
Measure the time taken (how long the reaction takes).
Stop the timer when the cross is obscured.
worked_example.tip: The second and third marks depend on placing the flask over a cross.

worked_example.question:
A student investigates the reaction between marble chips and hydrochloric acid. She times how long it takes for all the marble chips to react. Here are her results.

Experiment | Size of marble chips | Reaction time (s) | Mean rate of reaction (g/s)
1 | large | 240 | 8.33 × 10⁻⁴
2 | large | 120 | (blank)
3 | large | 100 | 2.00 × 10⁻³
4 | small | 50 | 4.00 × 10⁻³

Calculate the mean rate of reaction in experiment 2.

Give your answer to 3 significant figures and in standard form.
answer_points: Mass of marble = rate × time = 8.33 × 10⁻⁴ × 240 = 0.2 g (2 marks), or 100 × 2.00 × 10⁻³ = 0.2 g.
Mean rate = 1.67 × 10⁻³ g/s.
worked_example.tip: The answer 1.67 × 10⁻³ g/s scores all 3 marks.

worked_example.question:
A student investigates how the rate of reaction between dilute hydrochloric acid and aqueous sodium thiosulfate changes as the concentration of the thiosulfate decreases. The solution slowly becomes cloudy, so it becomes more difficult to see through it.

In Experiment 1, the student pours 50 cm³ of aqueous sodium thiosulfate into a 100 cm³ beaker and adds 5 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid. The student starts a stop-watch and stands the beaker on a printed sheet, looking down from above. The stop-watch is stopped when the text on the sheet is no longer visible.

Explain why it is important not to change to a larger beaker during the investigation.
answer_points: A different size of beaker would change the depth of solution (M1)
so the time measured would change (M2)
worked_example.tip: One mark for the change in depth and one for the effect on the time measured.

blocks.text: (Supplement) Judge each method by how accurate it is and when it suits a reaction.

rows: Gas syringe
It reads the volume of gas directly, in small steps.
Some gas escapes before the bung is put back on.
Gas collected over water
It is simple to set up.
A gas that dissolves in water, such as carbon dioxide, gives a volume that is too low.
Mass lost on a balance
A balance reads small changes in mass precisely, so it suits a gas with a large mass, such as carbon dioxide.
It fails for a light gas such as hydrogen, because the mass lost is too small to measure.

items: To stop gas escaping at the start, put one reagent in a small tube inside the flask. Tip the flask to start the reaction.
Cotton wool in the neck of a flask on a balance lets the gas escape but stops spray leaving the flask.
A cross that disappears is judged by eye, so it depends on the person. Use the same beaker, the same depth of liquid and the same observer.
Measure volumes with a burette rather than a measuring cylinder to be more accurate. Repeat the experiment and find a mean.

worked_example.question:
A student investigates the rate of reaction when hydrogen peroxide solution decomposes in a conical flask, collecting the gas that is made.

2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂

These solids catalyse the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide solution:
• lead(IV) oxide
• manganese(IV) oxide

Describe a method that the student could use to find out which solid is the more effective catalyst.
answer_points: Add hydrogen peroxide solution to the conical flask and add one of the catalysts (M1)
Record the time taken to collect a fixed volume of gas, or the volume of gas collected in a fixed time (M2)
Any two from: repeat with the same volume and concentration of hydrogen peroxide solution (M3); at the same temperature (M4); using the same mass of each catalyst (M5)
The more effective catalyst gives the greater volume of gas per unit time, or takes the least time to make a fixed volume of oxygen (M6)
worked_example.tip: Two marks are for the method, two for any two controlled variables and one for the conclusion.

blocks.text: Hydrogen peroxide breaks down slowly to make oxygen. A solid catalyst speeds this up.

items.text: Put a fixed volume of hydrogen peroxide solution in a conical flask connected to a gas syringe.
Add a measured mass of one solid, such as manganese(IV) oxide, and start the stopwatch.
Record the volume of oxygen at set times, or the time to collect a fixed volume.
Repeat with the same mass of other solids. Keep the volume, concentration and temperature the same.

items: The more effective catalyst gives more gas in the same time, or takes less time to collect a fixed volume.
A catalyst is not used up, so its mass is the same at the end.
